q: Leaving the marina at Kalamata for the open sea, you have this buoy ahead. On which side do you leave it?

a: A port-hand mark: leave it to port
o: A starboard-hand mark: leave it to starboard

A special mark: check the chart

fig.note: IALA region B · entering from sea

o: On the side away from the shore

q: You are sailing south through a channel between two islands, with no harbour at either end. How do you know which lateral marks are "port-hand"?
a: From the direction-of-buoyage arrow on the chart
o: Port is the side nearer the mainland
Port marks are always on the west side
From the direction you happen to sail
why: Lateral marks follow the direction of buoyage: from seaward, or as shown by the arrow on the chart.

o: To port: leave the mark to starboard
Straight past it: it is a safe water mark

o: Preferred channel to starboard: leave it to port
Isolated danger: pass on any side
why: Region A: Fl(2+1) G is a modified starboard-hand mark, so the main channel is to port.

fig.note: Night · channel junction, entering from sea

q: Your next charter is in the Philippines. Entering a harbour from sea, what colour are the lateral marks you keep on your starboard side?
a: Red
why: The Philippines, like the Americas, Japan and Korea, use IALA region B: red to starboard returning.

a: Alter to starboard and leave it to port
o: Hold on and leave it to starboard
Alter to port and pass close to it
why: Region A: a red light is a port-hand mark, so going in it must pass down your port side.

fig.note: Night · entering from sea · light fine to starboard

q: On the way into a marina at night, you see this light. What is it?
a: A starboard-hand lateral mark

fig.note: Night · channel into the marina

a: East of it
o: Any side, the danger is right under it

q: This mark stands off a reef near Hvar. Where do you pass it?
a: To the west of it
why: West cardinal: yellow–black–yellow, cones point to point; safe water to the west.

q: At night you see this light low on the water ahead. Which side of it is safe?
a: The east side
why: Three quick flashes = 3 o'clock = east cardinal.

fig.note: Night · light low on the water

q: Your track north runs close past this mark. How do you get by it safely?
a: Alter to port and leave it to starboard
o: Hold course and leave it to port
Alter to starboard and pass east of it

fig.note: Depths in metres · heading 000°

q: Approaching the Kornati islands at night, you see this light marking a shoal. Where do you pass it?
a: To the north
why: Uninterrupted quick or very quick flashing: north cardinal.

fig.note: Night · continuous, about two flashes a second

q: At dusk you can only see a dark silhouette on the buoy: two cones, one above the other, base to base. What mark is it?
a: An east cardinal
why: Base to base looks like an egg: E. Point to point: W. Both up: N. Both down: S.

q: Counting the quick flashes of a white light, you are not sure whether there were six or nine. What tells you it is a south cardinal?
a: A long flash follows the quick ones
o: There is no pause between groups
The pause after the group is shorter
why: South cardinal: Q(6) + LFl; the long flash stops it being mistaken for a west (Q(9)).

q: Bound west along the coast, which way do you take this mark?
a: Alter to starboard and leave it to port
o: Hold course and leave it to starboard
Alter to port and pass close south of it
why: North cardinal: safe water to the north; the danger lies south of it, on your track.

fig.note: Depths in metres · heading 270°

q: Sailing in the Bahamas (IALA region B), you see this mark. What does it mean there?
a: Pass to the east, as in region A
o: Pass to the west, colours are reversed in B
It is a starboard-hand mark in B
why: Only lateral marks differ between regions A and B; cardinals are the same worldwide.

fig.note: IALA region B

q: You want to continue east. Can you pass between these two marks?
a: No: go north of the N mark or south of the S mark
o: Yes: the gap between them is the channel
Yes, but only at slow speed
No: go west of both marks
why: Cardinals are named for where the safe water is, so the shoal lies between them.

fig.note: Depths in metres · you are heading east

q: Rounding a headland in the Gulf of Corinth, you see this mark off the point. Where is the danger?
a: North of the mark
why: South cardinal: safe water to the south, so the danger lies to the north of it.

q: You time this light on a buoy off Paros. Where do you pass it?
a: To the west
why: Nine quick flashes = 9 o'clock = west cardinal.

fig.note: Night · 9 quick flashes, then dark, every 15 s

q: The topmark of this buoy has been knocked off. It is painted yellow above black. Which mark is it?
a: A south cardinal: pass south
why: Cones point to the black: black at the bottom means both points down, south.

q: At night this light marks a rock in the middle of a bay. What is it?
a: An isolated danger mark: pass well clear, any side
o: A south cardinal: pass south of it
A port-hand mark: leave it to port
A safe water mark: steer for it
why: White Fl(2): isolated danger, with navigable water all round.

fig.note: Night · light on a beacon in the bay

q: Making landfall at night, you see this light ahead, low on the water, alone in open sea. What is it?
a: A safe water mark
why: White Iso, Oc, LFl 10s or Mo(A): safe water — landfall or mid-channel.

fig.note: Night · approaching from offshore

q: At dusk you see a pillar buoy with a single ball as its topmark. What kind of mark is it?
a: A safe water mark
why: One red ball: safe water. Two black balls: isolated danger.

q: Anchoring off a beach in Zakynthos, you see a line of these buoys between you and the shore. What do they usually mark?
a: The edge of a swimming area: stay outside
o: A channel for yachts to the beach
The edge of a dredged channel
why: Yellow special marks along beaches usually mark the bathing zone; check the chart or local rules.

fig.note: Small buoys in a line parallel to the beach

a: A fish farm: keep outside them

a: An emergency wreck-marking buoy
o: A special mark on a fish farm

fig.note: Night · one light: blue, then yellow, then blue…

a: A newly found danger, marked with a duplicate
o: One of them has dragged: ignore it
A practice area for buoy tenders
why: IALA: a serious new danger may be marked by duplicating one of the marks until it is charted.

fig.note: Two of these, side by side; chart shows clear water

fig.note: Chart extract

o: Mostly dark, with two short flashes every 8 s
Equal light and dark, twice every 8 s
Two long flashes, each lasting 8 s
why: Oc: light longer than dark; Oc(2) 8s puts two eclipses in each 8-second period.

fig.note: Chart extract

q: Which chart abbreviation matches the harbour light your crew is timing?

a: The height of the light above sea level
o: The height of the tower from its base
The least depth off the cape
The width of the red sector

o: The distance to the next light

The width of its white and red sectors
why: Nominal range in 10 M visibility: 18 M for the white, 15 M for the weaker red.

fig.note: Chart extract

o: You cannot tell without its colour

a: B

o: Alter to starboard until it shows white

Stop and wait until it shows red

q: What do these lights tell you?

o: A large power vessel showing her port side

A sailing vessel showing her port side
